title: The history of the electric scooter
tagline: Two hundred years from Faraday's spinning wire to millions of Indian scooters with a motor in the back wheel.
intro: The electric scooter needed three inventions: a motor, a battery you can recharge, and electronics to link them. The motor came first, in 1821, and inventors were fitting motors inside bicycle wheels by 1895. But lead-acid batteries were heavy, and petrol won the century. Then transistors replaced brushes, neodymium magnets made motors strong and light, and the lithium-ion cell packed energy into a small can. In India, government schemes paid part of the price, and fires in 2022 made battery safety rules much stricter.

eras.name: Motors and batteries are born
eras.summary: Scientists make the first electric motors and the first rechargeable battery, and inventors bolt them onto tricycles and bicycles.

eras.name: Motors in the wheel
eras.summary: Patents put the motor inside the wheel hub, but heavy lead-acid batteries keep electric two-wheelers a curiosity while petrol takes over.

eras.name: Magnets, chips and lithium
eras.summary: Transistors replace brushes, powerful neodymium magnets arrive, and the lithium-ion cell is invented and sold.

eras.name: Electric two-wheelers take off
eras.summary: Pedal-assist bikes in Japan, hundreds of millions of e-bikes in China, and India's first electric scooters, many on lead-acid batteries.

eras.name: India goes electric
eras.summary: Government schemes pay part of the price, lithium-ion scooters spread, fires in 2022 bring tougher battery rules, and shared kick scooters fill city streets worldwide.

events.title: A wire that spins round a magnet
events.text: Faraday hung a wire carrying current next to a magnet in a cup of mercury, and the wire went round and round. It was the first device to turn electricity into continuous motion.
events.why: Every electric scooter motor still works by the push between a current and a magnet.

events.title: The first patented electric motor
events.text: Davenport, a blacksmith, built a rotating motor with electromagnets and received a US patent in 1837. Batteries of the day were too weak and costly for it to succeed in business.
events.why: It showed motors could do real work; batteries had to catch up.

events.title: The rechargeable battery
events.text: Planté rolled two lead sheets with a separator into acid and found he could charge and recharge the cell. Improved lead-acid batteries powered the first electric vehicles and early Indian electric scooters.
events.why: For a century, lead-acid was the only practical rechargeable battery.

events.title: An electric tricycle on the streets of Paris
events.text: Trouvé fitted a small motor of his own design and rechargeable lead-acid batteries to an English tricycle and drove it along a Paris street. It is often called the first electric vehicle of its kind.
events.why: The basic recipe of battery, motor and wheels was in place.

events.title: A motor inside the back wheel
events.text: Bolton was granted a US patent for a battery-powered bicycle with a direct-current motor built into the hub of the rear wheel, the battery hung under the frame. Whether it was ever made for sale is not known.
events.why: It is the ancestor of the hub motor in today's scooters.

events.title: Two motors and a choice of batteries
events.text: Libbey patented an electric bicycle driven by a double motor set in the crank hub (attributed; early e-bike patents came thick and fast in the 1890s).
events.why: Inventors tried many places for the motor: hub, crank and belt.

events.title: Hub motors on a car
events.text: The Lohner–Porsche car shown in Paris had electric motors inside its front wheel hubs, with no gears or chains. It was heavy, because of its lead-acid batteries.
events.why: The in-wheel motor idea reached cars; scooters use it today.

events.title: Switches instead of brushes
events.who: T. G. Wilson and P. H. Trickey
events.text: Wilson and Trickey described a DC machine with 'solid-state commutation': transistors, not rubbing brushes, switched the current in its coils (widely cited as the start of the brushless DC motor).
events.why: The controller in every e-scooter does this switching.

events.title: A lithium battery that recharges
events.text: Whittingham built a rechargeable lithium battery with a titanium disulphide electrode that stored lithium ions between its layers. It gave about 2 V but lithium metal made it risky.
events.why: It started the race to the lithium-ion cell.

events.title: A better cathode: cobalt oxide
events.text: Goodenough's team showed that lithium cobalt oxide could take in and give out lithium ions at about 4 V, nearly twice Whittingham's battery.
events.why: Higher voltage means more energy in every cell.

events.title: Neodymium magnets
events.who: Masato Sagawa (Sumitomo) and John Croat (General Motors)
events.text: Two teams independently found that an alloy of neodymium, iron and boron makes the strongest permanent magnets known. They were announced in 1984.
events.why: Strong, light magnets make small hub motors powerful.

events.title: The first lithium-ion cell
events.text: Yoshino paired Goodenough's cathode with a carbon anode that holds lithium ions, with no lithium metal at all. The cell was lighter, safer and could be recharged hundreds of times.
events.why: This is the cell inside every e-scooter pack.

events.title: Lithium-ion goes on sale
events.text: Sony began selling lithium-ion cells in 1991, first for video cameras and then phones and laptops.
events.why: Mass production made the cells cheap enough, decades later, for vehicles.

events.title: The power-assist bicycle
events.text: Yamaha launched the PAS, a bicycle whose motor helps only while you pedal. Pedal-assist e-bikes, limited to about 24–25 km/h, became a big market in Japan and later Europe.
events.why: Low-speed, low-power electric bikes got their own rules.

events.title: Hundreds of millions of e-bikes in China
events.text: As some Chinese cities restricted petrol motorcycles, cheap electric bikes and scooters with hub motors and lead-acid batteries spread fast; China became by far the largest e-two-wheeler market.
events.why: It made hub motors and controllers cheap for the world.

events.title: India's FAME scheme
events.text: FAME India (Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles) began paying part of the price of electric and hybrid vehicles, including two-wheelers.
events.why: It was the first national push to make Indians buy electric.

events.title: Shared e-scooters by the minute
events.text: Dockless electric kick scooters that anyone could unlock with a phone appeared in Santa Monica in 2017 and spread to hundreds of cities within two years. Many cities later capped their speed or limited them.
events.why: Kick scooters became an everyday sight, and a new rule-making headache.

events.title: FAME II: money per kWh
events.text: FAME II started with an outlay of ₹10,000 crore. Electric two-wheelers got ₹10,000 per kWh of battery, so a bigger pack earned a bigger incentive, for scooters that met range, speed and local-content rules.
events.why: Paying by battery size tied the subsidy to the part that matters most.

events.title: Nobel Prize for the lithium-ion battery
events.who: John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, Akira Yoshino
events.text: The three shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 'for the development of lithium-ion batteries'. Goodenough, at 97, became the oldest Nobel laureate.
events.why: The cell in your scooter earned science's top prize.

events.title: Subsidy raised to ₹15,000 per kWh
events.text: The FAME II incentive for electric two-wheelers rose from ₹10,000 to ₹15,000 per kWh, capped at 40% of the vehicle's cost, and the scheme was extended to March 2024. Sales of electric scooters rose sharply.
events.why: Cheaper scooters brought electric two-wheelers to the mass market.

events.title: BIS-certified helmets only
events.who: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
events.text: A quality control order made BIS certification to IS 4151:2015 compulsory for two-wheeler riders' helmets; selling uncertified ones became an offence.
events.why: Every e-scooter rider and pillion must wear a certified helmet.

events.title: A string of scooter fires
events.text: Several electric scooters caught fire in a few weeks, some while charging, and lives were lost. MoRTH set up an expert committee, and DRDO's fire-safety centre (CFEES) investigated; reports pointed to cell, BMS and pack-design faults.
events.why: It showed how much depends on good cells, a good BMS and testing.

events.title: A draft battery-swapping policy
events.text: After a Budget promise in February 2022, NITI Aayog published a draft policy for swapping a flat battery for a charged one at a station, with interoperability standards. It was a draft for public comment.
events.why: Swapping could turn hours of charging into minutes.

events.title: Tougher battery rules: AIS-156
events.who: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
events.text: MoRTH amended the AIS-156 standard for electric two- and three-wheelers. Phase 1, from 1 December 2022, added traceable cells, cell spacing, a microcontroller BMS and an extra fuse; Phase 2, from 31 March 2023, added temperature sensors and a warning for thermal events.
events.why: Every new scooter's pack must pass these tests.

events.title: Subsidy cut
events.text: The FAME II incentive for electric two-wheelers fell to ₹10,000 per kWh and the cap to 15% of the ex-factory price.
events.why: Scooter prices rose; makers began cutting costs and adding cheaper models.

events.title: Paris votes out rental e-scooters
events.text: In a city vote, Parisians chose to end shared rental e-scooters; the operators left the city that September.
events.why: Cities kept debating where kick scooters belong.

events.title: PM E-DRIVE
events.who: Union Cabinet, Ministry of Heavy Industries
events.text: The Cabinet approved PM E-DRIVE with an outlay of ₹10,900 crore, replacing FAME II and a stop-gap scheme (EMPS 2024). Electric two-wheelers got ₹5,000 per kWh, capped at ₹10,000, in its first year, then ₹2,500 per kWh, capped at ₹5,000.
events.why: Incentives began to taper as electric scooters got cheaper.

events.title: Incentives extended to 2028; low-speed rules reviewed
events.text: The government extended PM E-DRIVE's two-wheeler incentive to 31 March 2028 at ₹2,500 per kWh, capped at ₹5,000 (as reported). In August 2026 MoRTH also published a draft to raise the motor power limit for registration-free low-speed vehicles from 250 W to 600 W, keeping 25 km/h (a draft, not yet final when this box was made).
events.why: The rules are still being written as the technology changes.

series.title: Central incentive per kWh for an electric two-wheeler in India
series.caption: Under FAME II, EMPS and PM E-DRIVE, the Government of India paid buyers a fixed amount for each kWh of battery, with a cap per vehicle.

points.label: FAME II from April 2019: ₹10,000 per kWh, capped at 20% of cost
From June 2021: ₹15,000 per kWh, capped at 40%
From 1 June 2023: ₹10,000 per kWh, capped at 15%
EMPS 2024 and PM E-DRIVE year 1: ₹5,000 per kWh, capped at ₹10,000
PM E-DRIVE from April 2025: ₹2,500 per kWh, capped at ₹5,000 (extended to March 2028)

facts: A family e-scooter's battery holds about as much energy as a third of a litre of petrol, yet takes you around a hundred kilometres.
In a hub motor the magnets turn and the coils stay still, the opposite of most motors you see in fans.
John Goodenough was 97 when he won the Nobel Prize for the lithium-ion battery, the oldest Nobel laureate ever.
Stopping from 40 km/h, a scooter and rider hold only about 3 watt-hours of motion energy, less than a fifth of what a smartphone battery stores.
India's subsidies were paid per kWh of battery, so the battery, not the badge, decided the discount.
